analysis.explanation: The Random Forest classified this binary as malware with probability 0.9950, and all 20 top SHAP features push toward cryptojacking. No feature opposes the prediction. The contributions are spread fairly evenly (+0.0063 to +0.0128) rather than dominated by one feature, so the verdict rests on a broad pattern. The strongest feature is PXOR MOVUPS (+0.012849), at the highest frequency among the specific SIMD patterns (0.001144). It is reinforced by PXOR PXOR (+0.008992), LEA PXOR (+0.007483), CVTSI2SD PXOR (+0.006602), MOVQ PUNPCKLQDQ (+0.007867) and ADD MOVQ (+0.007014). Together these indicate heavy SSE register clearing, vector loads and 64-bit lane packing, which is typical of vectorized mixing or hashing loops. A second group is bit-manipulation and carry arithmetic: XOR ADC (+0.008959), SHL NEG (+0.009045), ROL MOVZX (+0.006801), ADD ROR (+0.006597), SAR JNZ (+0.006744), MOVSXD BSR (+0.006780) and SUB CMOVG (+0.010716). This is consistent with rotate/XOR/add hash rounds and multi-precision arithmetic. A third group is x87 floating-point traffic (FSTP MOV, MOV FLD, ADD FLD, FSTP FSTP; +0.0066 to +0.0123). It is less specific to mining and may reflect general numeric code, but the model weights it toward malware. Caveats: the n-grams are generic mnemonic pairs that ordinary compiled code can also produce, and the evidence lists no function names, API references or strings. The classification therefore depends on the model's aggregate statistical signal, not on any directly identifiable mining routine. The consistent direction and magnitude of the signal still support a high-confidence call, with moderated certainty.

evidence_analysis.assessment: Top feature. Zeroing an SSE register followed by an unaligned vector load/store suggests buffer initialization or block-wise processing of wide data, as in vectorized hashing or scratchpad handling. At 0.001144 it is among the most frequent of the specific patterns.
x87 store-and-pop followed by an integer move. It is very rare (0.000009) but heavily weighted, so it may be a distinctive marker. On its own it is not clearly mining-specific.

Subtract followed by a conditional move is branchless clamping or comparison logic, common in optimized arithmetic and difficulty/target-style comparisons. Interpretation is speculative; the model weights it strongly.
Shift-and-negate is a bit-masking idiom used in low-level arithmetic and bit manipulation. It is rare (0.000004) but weighted toward malware.
Consecutive SSE XORs suggest vectorized XOR mixing or register zeroing, in line with the SIMD-heavy profile seen in hash computation.
XOR followed by add-with-carry points to multi-word arithmetic or mixing operations. Moderate frequency (0.000314) suggests repeated use.
Loading data to the x87 FPU. Together with the other FLD/FSTP patterns it indicates notable x87 floating-point usage. This is not itself a mining marker, but the model treats it as indicative.
A generic call/stack-setup sequence. Alone it is weak, but the model assigns it notable positive weight, possibly reflecting code-structure characteristics common to the malware class.
Moving a 64-bit value and packing it into the low quadword of an SSE register is typical of SIMD data shuffling used in vectorized state handling. Relatively frequent (0.000370).
Address computation followed by a repeated string move is bulk memory copy or initialization, plausibly large buffer handling. Rare (0.000006).
Address calculation followed by SSE XOR suggests vector operations on computed memory locations, adding to the SIMD-processing profile.
Integer addition followed by a 64-bit SSE move, consistent with mixed scalar/vector arithmetic. Moderate frequency (0.000242) suggests recurring use.
A rotate followed by a zero-extending move is a rotate-and-extract idiom common in hash and cipher rounds and byte-wise table lookups.
Sign-extending a 32-bit value and scanning for the highest set bit is bit-length computation, as in big-number or normalization arithmetic. Rare but weighted toward malware.
An arithmetic shift followed by a conditional branch is a bit-testing loop construct. It is generic but contributes to the profile of bit-level processing.
Integer add followed by an x87 load. It reinforces the x87 floating-point usage seen in other features and is not strongly mining-specific on its own.

Integer-to-double conversion followed by an SSE register clear is a standard compiler idiom for floating-point conversion. Its weight suggests the model sees it as part of the malware numeric profile, though it is weak evidence by itself.
Add followed by rotate-right is a classic add-rotate-xor round pattern in hash and cipher primitives. This is one of the more mining-relevant bit-manipulation signals.
Back-to-back x87 store-and-pop operations indicate sequential FPU result handling. Together with the FLD patterns it forms a distinct x87 cluster.

Masking followed by subtraction is a common arithmetic and alignment idiom. It has the highest frequency in the list (0.001372), so it likely reflects pervasive code style, and it adds modest positive weight.

Rotate, shift and carry-arithmetic idioms (ADD ROR, ROL MOVZX, XOR ADC, SHL NEG, SAR JNZ) typical of hash-round and multi-precision computation
Branchless comparison and bit-scan patterns (SUB CMOVG, MOVSXD BSR)
Cluster of x87 floating-point patterns (FSTP MOV, MOV FLD, ADD FLD, FSTP FSTP) weighted toward malware
Limitation: no function-level, API or string evidence was provided, and the n-grams are generic mnemonic pairs, so the verdict relies on aggregate statistical signal
analysis.recommended_action: Treat as a probable cryptojacker and escalate. Perform dynamic analysis in a sandbox to look for sustained CPU load, mining-pool network connections and persistence. Statically locate the functions containing the PXOR/MOVUPS and rotate/XOR/ADC sequences and check whether they implement a hashing loop. Since function-level evidence was not supplied, confirm with disassembly, strings and network indicators before final attribution.
